title: Two-Step Crystal Nucleation in a Metallic Glass Super Cooled Liquid Using In-Situ 4D STEM
content: Nanobeam diffraction measures effectively short and medium range order within disordered materials. The 0.5- 2 nm electron beam matches the short- to medium-range ordering length scale in disordered supercooled liquids and glasses [1,2]. The resultant nanobeam diffraction patterns probe local symmetry and can be used to measure the relative degree of ordering within structures[3–5]. Rastering this probe across the sample and acquiring a nanobeam diffraction pattern at each position (4D STEM) gives spatial information about the structures which can be used to segment and cluster strong diffraction[6]. With the advent of ultrafast detectors for 4D STEM, time resolved, in-situ 4D STEM experiments are now possible with the ability to acquire a modest 4D STEM dataset in 1-10 seconds[7]. We have used a Direct Electron CeleritasXS camera and a DENS Wildfire heating holder to acquire a series of in-situ 4D STEM datasets measuring nucleation from a supercooled liquid. The data reveal a two-step process crystal nucleation process. First, disordered fluctuating structures form within the supercooled liquid, and second, from within one of the disordered fluctuating structures an ordered crystal nucleates and grows.
